title: Oil Cracks $100 as US-Iran War Grinds On
excerpt: Brent crude has surged over 55% since February as the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively shut, threatening global growth and inflation.
body:
Oil markets crossed the psychologically critical $100-a-barrel threshold this week, driven by the continuing US-Iran war that began on February 28, 2026, when joint American and Israeli airstrikes triggered the biggest energy crisis the modern world has ever seen.

**What happened:**
Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading at $105 a barrel, up 44% since before the war started. Brent has surged more than 55% since the Iran war began, hitting nearly $120 a barrel at its peak, amid fears of disrupted oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has caused the restriction of nearly all traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, leading to what the International Energy Agency has characterised as the 'largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market'.

**Why it matters globally:**
The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage of the Persian Gulf through which a fifth of the world's crude oil normally passes, has effectively been shut, and oil tankers have been stranded there unable to deliver crude. Royal Bank of Canada warns that a sustained oil price of $100 per barrel would keep US inflation above 3 percent for the remainder of the year. Fourth-quarter-over-fourth-quarter global real GDP growth in 2026 could fall 0.2 percentage points if the oil supply disruption remains limited to one quarter, or 0.3 percentage points if it lasts two quarters, rising to 1.3 percentage points if the disruption persists for three quarters.

**What to watch:**
Officials in Washington and Tehran were working on 'a one-page memorandum of understanding to end the war and set a framework for more detailed nuclear negotiations,' but any reopening of the strait would likely trigger an immediate drop of between $10 and $20 in crude prices due to speculative positioning — watch for a deal or a breakdown in talks as the decisive market trigger.

nri_angle: India is among the top importers of Hormuz crude — with the Indian Navy already escorting LPG carriers through the Gulf under Operation Sankalp — making every spike in oil prices a direct hit on India's economy, remittances, and the cost of living for families Indian-Americans support back home.
